newsitem.title: INDIA: Political woes seen rattling Indian shares.
newsitem.headline: Political woes seen rattling Indian shares.

text.p: Concerns about India's fragile minority coalition government's survival are likely to depress share prices this week, analysts said.
"It looks pretty bad," said Bimal Parekh, senior dealer at Bombay brokerage P.R. Subramanyan & Sons. "I would advise my clients to stay away."
Simmering discontent among the 15-party ruling United Front coalition comprising regional parties, communists and free-market advocates, has raised the prospect of a snap election, analysts said.
"A snap poll cannot be ruled out," said one analyst at a foreign brokerage. "It could spoil the party in the near-term."

Last week the 30-share Bombay Stock Exchange index plunged 197.17 points or five percent to 4,124.81, the biggest week-to-week fall in 1997, as fresh political tensions hit late in the week. It had hit 33-month highs of 4,448.06 a week earlier, helped by strong foreign inflows.
Analysts expect the index to slide another 100-200 points this week on political worries.
"We'll see panic if the index slips under 4,000," said Arun Kejriwal, an independent market analyst. "It could take it down to 3,900."
Nilesh Shah, research head at N.H. Securities, said the market could tumble to 3,850 if the government fell apart.

In the latest of its year-long troubles, the United Front government was rattled last week when a southern regional party threatened to pull out four of its nominees in the cabinet, including Industry Minister Murasoli Maran.
The shaky coalition has been hit by corruption and Hindu nationalism.

Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral has declined to recognise a breakaway group of his own party. The group's leader faces corruption charges in court. At least three supporters of that group are ministers in the government.

Also, a lack of consensus within the coalition has undermined the government's bid to resolve its pricing policy for oil. Prolonged uncertainty over the policy was affecting the liquidity position of oil companies and the inflow of new investments into the sector, officials have said.
A foreign fund manager said that long-term investors should have few concerns about Indian markets which have been the best performing in Asia this year.
"All major political parties are committed to globally oriented reforms," said Richard Overton, managing director of ITC Classic Threadneedle Asset Management Company Ltd which manages a mutual fund.
He said the market was driven by abundant liquidity caused by lower interest rates and equities continued to be an attractive investment.
Analysts said foreign portfolio investments in blue-chip firms were expected to reach government-set ceilings and could result in a slowing of fresh inflows.

Shares of Housing Development Finance Corporation Ltd sagged 780 rupees, or 16.6 percent, to 3,923.25 in two days last week after the central bank said foreign portfolio holdings had hit the 30 percent ceiling.
